newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: FORECAST - Irish credit growth to accelerate in Sept.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Irish credit growth to accelerate in Sept.

text.p: A majority of analysts expect Irish private sector credit growth to have accelerated again in September while they believe external reserves may have risen to as much six billion punts by the end of that month.
Forecasts for underlying credit growth, due for release at 1630 GMT on Thursday, range from 14.1 percent to 14.8 percent compared with a growth rate of 14.3 percent in August.
Five out of eight analysts surveyed are expecting a rise.
"There has been an underlying upward trend in private sector credit growth since February," said Oliver Mangan, economist at Davy Stockbrokers who expects a growth rate of 14.8 percent.

"Judging by recent months, there has not been much sign of a deceleration and the anecdotal evidence we have from talking to building societies and banks is that lending activity in September remained robust, that the housing market remained buoyant and house-building activity remained buoyant."
Analysts say a small rise in lending rates at the end of August was unlikely to have depressed consumer demand.

"The small increase of 25 basis points has done little to dampen consumers' spirits. Indeed, we believe that credit demand will keep on growing until the bank take further corrective action," said Alan McQuaid of Bloxham Stockbrokers, who is forecasting a 14.5 percent increase in private sector credit.
Even Goodbody Stockbrokers, whose 14.1 estimate is at the lowest end of the range, says its forecast is due to base effects rather than a real deceleration in lending.
"We are coming off strong growth at the same time last year which is causing the apparent slowdown," Goodbody's Jenny Pollock said.
But Riada Stockbrokers, who are forecasting a 14.2 percent increase in private sector credit growth, believe there are signs that demand is levelling off.

"There is some evidence that retail sales may be slowing back if you believe the official data and there is some evidence that the credit numbers may be set for a slowdown," analyst Padhraic Garvey told Reuters.

Economists say a strong figure is probably priced into the market but growth above 14.8 percent would cause nervousness and interbank rates would probably tighten while the short end of the bond market would underperform.

"I don't think too much notice will be taken if it comes in around 14.8 percent but obviously if it's stronger than that, there would be significant reaction at the short end of the cash market," said Pat O'Sullivan, economist at AIB Capital Markets.

But unless the figure is significantly outside expectations, analysts say there is little chance of any official rise in Irish interest rates given Irish pound strength in the ERM and the central bank's desire to be seen to be following German rather than British interest rates ahead of EMU.
Analysts will also be keeping a close eye on the external foreign reserves, to be released with the lending data, given recent developments in the foreign exchange market.
The Irish pound has plunged by 4.5 percent against sterling in the last three months and dipped below parity last week, provoking central bank intervention to support it.
"Evidence of the extent of punt selling from the foreign exchange data will be interesting, especially in light of the recent reversal to net punt buying," Riada Stockbrokers says.

Analysts believe the bank has a sizable arsenal with which to defend the currency and forecasts for the end-September reserves range from 5.35 billion to 6.0 billion compared with 5.15 billion at end-August.
"I have provisionally put in a rise of 650 million punts taking the reserves up to 5.8 billion but a figure of 6.0 billion wouldn't surprise me," said Davy's Mangan.
"All the indications are that central bank selling of the Irish pound was substantial in September."
